extracted.intended_audience: writers, students, and anyone learning grammar or narrative point of view
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for identifying and using first-, second-, and third-person points of view in writing, including pronoun cues, examples, and distinctions among third-person subtypes (limited, omniscient, objective).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing a clear point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing a clear point of view is essential because it dictates how readers interpret characters, events, ideas, and other important details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and maintain a consistent perspective so readers understand whose eyes the story is told through; the chosen POV affects presentation and reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Point of view in writing refers to the perspective from which a story or piece of text is narrated — whose eyes a story is told through.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this concept to decide how information is presented and how readers will interpret and engage with the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: In first-person point of view, the speaker refers to themself or a group they’re included in; uses first-person pronouns (I, me, my, mine, myself; we, us, our, ourselves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a personal and subjective experience, allowing readers to see and feel the story directly from the narrator’s perspective. Examples: "I think I lost my wallet!"; "When I fall asleep, I can still see the sunlight on the waves." Note: singular 'they' is not first person — it is grammatically third person even when used for a singular referent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-person point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Second-person point of view addresses the person (or people) being spoken to — the you perspective; indicated by pronouns like you, your, yours, yourself, yourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directly addresses the reader and can make them feel part of the story; commonly used in instructional writing. Examples: "You can wait in here and make yourself at home." Stories written in second person exist but are much rarer than first- or third-person narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-person point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: In third-person point of view, the narrator talks about someone or something else (the third person); uses pronouns such as he, she, they, it and related forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reads as an outside observer describing characters by name or third-person pronouns; common for stories and novels. Example: "Tiffany used her prize money..."

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-person limited
rubrics_metrics.description: A subtype of third-person narration that focuses closely on the thoughts, feelings, and experiences of one character but from an outside perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives readers access to one character’s inner life while retaining the external narrator stance. Example: "Tom watched the sunrise, feeling a mix of hope and sadness..."

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-person omniscient
rubrics_metrics.description: A subtype where the narrator knows all the thoughts, actions, and feelings of every character, providing an all-knowing overview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows the narrator to move between characters’ minds and provide information beyond any single character’s knowledge. Example: "Sally hoped for a promotion, unaware that John... planned to resign that very day."

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-person objective
rubrics_metrics.description: A subtype in which the narrator reports actions and dialogue without delving into the thoughts or feelings of any characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offers a detached, reportage-like viewpoint that shows external behavior without internal access. Example: "The cat sat on the windowsill, watching as the rain poured down..."

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying point of view without pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all sentences include pronouns, especially in third person; you can determine POV by considering whether the narrator is the speaker, the addressee, or someone being talked about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use elimination: if you think "Mike isn’t me," eliminate first person; if you’re not talking to Mike, eliminate second person — you’re left with third person. Example: "Mike always hated school."

rubrics_metrics.name: Using point of view effectively / choosing the best POV
rubrics_metrics.description: Using point of view effectively involves choosing the perspective that best suits the narrative and the way you want to connect with readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember each POV offers a unique way to present ideas, characters, and plot; consider function (e.g., intimacy vs. distance, direct address vs. overview) when selecting POV. Also: speaking in the third person can be used sparingly for comedic effect or to grab attention (example dialogue demonstrating third-person self-reference).
